title: Mooncakes sell for only two months a year, yet they've become a 28.2 billion yuan business
dek: Being bound to Mid-Autumn Festival actually traps the mooncake's selling window, but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from the gifting occasion and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.
why: Worth listening for people in the food industry and anyone who wants to understand the holiday-consumption business, but information density is low — much of the runtime is spent on explaining regional styles and flavors, with the business mechanics concentrated in the middle and later sections.
who: Food industry founders, brands doing corporate custom gifts, and investors who want to understand the logic of holiday-consumption businesses.
skip: 0:12-2:03 — personal taste preferences and Taiwan date-paste pastry, unrelated to the business analysis.

points.h: Zongzi can sell year-round; mooncakes cannot
points.body: Zongzi is tied to Dragon Boat Festival, but once vacuum-sealed for long shelf life it can sell all year, and Wufangzhai even opened restaurants to put zongzi into everyday settings. The mooncake's problem isn't that the craft can't achieve long shelf life — it's that it's defined as a ‘traditional festival pastry mainly eaten during Mid-Autumn Festival’, and the national standard GB19855 writes the season directly into the definition. So of two festival foods, zongzi can decouple from its holiday through shelf life and channels, while mooncakes cannot.

points.h: The national standard draws hard lines on fillings
points.body: Lotus-paste mooncakes must contain no less than 60% lotus seeds, fruit mooncakes no less than 25% fruit products, and five-kernel mooncakes must use the five kernels: walnut, almond, olive kernel, melon seed, and sesame. The purpose of these lines is to push ingredient cost up and prevent cheap candied winter melon, red-and-green shreds, and low-grade nuts from being used as filler. For consumers, reading the order of the ingredient list is enough to judge how much is actually in there.

points.h: Why custard lava mooncakes are made so small
points.body: The small size of custard lava mooncakes isn't stinginess — it's structural. Outside is pastry, in the middle a custard layer, and at the center the lava layer, with the custard layer acting as a moisture barrier. Production requires two bakes to keep the lava semi-solid, and the lava's melting point has to be engineered — solid during transport, flowing liquid only after a few seconds in the microwave. Overheat it and the lava is absorbed by the crust, and it reverts to an ordinary custard mooncake.

points.h: Five preconditions for 'everything can be a mooncake'
points.body: Not everything can be stuffed into a mooncake. First, water content — hot-and-sour soup mooncakes are impossible because there's too much water to contain. Second, safety — meat, egg, and dairy are also what microbes like, so processing temperatures and sterilization processes must be tested repeatedly. Third, particle size — too large and the crust can't hold it, too fine and you can't taste it. Fourth, flavor retention after high-temperature baking — some aromas simply vanish once baked. Fifth, whether the cost can be handled. So a long-term stable flavor is something confirmed generation after generation.

points.h: Choosing an OEM isn't a matter of bigger is better
points.body: When big brands look for OEMs to make their branded mooncakes, there's a common misconception: you must pick the best OEM in the country. But a top-tier OEM's production scale actually doesn't match yours. Indicators you can screen on include registered capital, tax payment records, number of employees with social insurance contributions, and accumulated days of safe production. Also, the nine regional styles correspond to different factories — you can't ask Guangzhou Restaurant to produce Shanxi egg-skin mooncakes; they don't have that capability or production line.

points.h: Flexible lines can take orders of a few hundred boxes
points.body: Mooncake production is semi-automated and semi-manual: wrapping and forming can be done by machine, but brushing egg wash, pressing patterns, and stamping require hands, which actually makes it favorable for OEM and customization. Flexible factories can go as small as a few hundred boxes, and can do thousands or tens of thousands. If a company has only 50 employees, it can use the factory's existing mooncakes directly and only needs to design the box. This small-batch, fast-response capability is the core of why mooncakes can support a corporate customization business.

points.h: The 28.2 billion yuan scale is propped up by gifting
points.body: In 2025 China's mooncake output was 518,000 tons and sales scale 28.2 billion RMB, both down from the previous year. At 80 grams each that's about 6.4 billion pieces; at 100 grams, about 5.18 billion. Across a population of 1.4 billion, that's three to four per person on average. For comparison, Dragon Boat Festival zongzi annual sales are about 10 to 11 billion, and instant noodles about 68 to 120 billion. That mooncakes can do 28.2 billion selling only two months a year comes down to the gifting attribute — brands prepare large volumes of PR gifts at the two nodes of Chinese New Year and Mid-Autumn, and zongzi's gifting attribute is far weaker than the mooncake's.

points.h: 499 yuan is a number forced out by the regulatory line
points.body: In 2022 the National Development and Reform Commission and three other departments jointly issued an announcement placing boxed mooncakes priced above 500 yuan per unit under key supervision. So the highest price on the market is 499. The calculation logic: a box of mooncakes costs about 70 yuan per box, and adding channel commissions and allocated expenses, it can't exceed 500. Back when the economy was good there were sky-high mooncakes with very expensive tea or liquor inside, even wooden gift boxes, with both cost and price very high.

points.h: Mini package is becoming the trend
points.body: In the food industry these past two years there's a clear trend called mini package — packaging made smaller. On one hand it can be finished in one sitting after opening; on the other, consumers just want a quick treat and don't want to eat that much, and small packaging also lets you buy many flavors at once. Mooncakes are moving in this direction too, because it's hard for one person to finish a whole mooncake — usually it's cut into several pieces to share. Made smaller, one person can at least finish one, and waste is reduced.

points.h: New flavors die before reaching consumers
points.body: Brands launch five new flavors a year to see which gets eliminated, but a flavor having no repeat purchase doesn't necessarily mean consumers dislike it — it may simply never have reached consumers. Because most mooncakes are gifts, constantly regifted and passed along, and the recipient never eats it before passing it on. So next year they won't want to buy that flavor either, because this year they never tasted it. The advantage of brands with physical stores is that they can do tastings, letting consumers try before deciding.

quotes.text: I think we have pastries and cakes 365 days a year — it's just that what we normally eat isn't called a mooncake.
It's not that everything can be forced into a mooncake. A long-term stable flavor is definitely something confirmed as OK generation after generation.
This big OEM's production scale actually doesn't match yours.
If it's pulled away from the Mid-Autumn time slot, or pulled away from the round shape, it's really just a pastry.
A flavor with no repeat purchase doesn't necessarily mean consumers dislike it — it may be that it never reached consumers at all.
Brands and channels alike no longer want to consider making a long-term classic that gets passed down forever. What everyone actually wants is rapid iteration.
